This page brings together South Surrey and

foreclosures and court ordered sales from the MLS in one place. In B.C., a foreclosure isn't a quick bank auction. It runs through the Supreme Court of British Columbia, and a judge approves the final sale. That means the steps, the paperwork and the timing work differently from a regular purchase. Here's a plain guide to how it works, so you know what to expect before you make an offer.

blocks.text: How a court ordered sale works in B.C.

parts.t: When a borrower falls behind, the lender can ask for all the mortgage money under the standard mortgage terms set under the Land Title Act. It can then go to court. Under the Supreme Court Civil Rules (Rule 21-7), a foreclosure has to be started by petition. Everyone whose interest in the property could be cut off is named in it. The petition is served with the court's information notice for foreclosures, Form 125.

blocks.text: The order nisi and the redemption period

parts.t: The court can make an order, called an order nisi, giving the owner a set time to pay what's owed. That time is the redemption period. The Rules don't set a fixed length for it. The court decides it in each case. If the owner doesn't pay by the end of it, the lender can ask for a final order of foreclosure.

Most of the time the property is sold rather than simply handed to the lender. The court can give one party, usually the lender, "conduct of sale". That party lists the property, often on the MLS, and deals with offers. The court can set how the sale happens, set a minimum price, and set the rules for bids and offers (Rule 13-5).

blocks.text: Your offer is subject to court approval

parts.t: When you buy a court ordered sale, your accepted offer is conditional on the court approving it. The party with conduct of sale applies to the court for an order that confirms the sale and vests title in you. That can happen even before the redemption period is over (Rule 21-7).

This is the part that surprises most people. Under the Supreme Court's Practice Direction 66, other buyers can bring sealed bids to the approval hearing. Sealed bids, with a copy of the proof of deposit, have to be collected in the courtroom by 9:45 a.m. on the day of the hearing. The judge decides how to deal with them, and can consider late bids. Approval hearings are generally held in person. So even with an accepted offer, you could be outbid in court. I'll help you plan for that.

A foreclosure is filed at the Supreme Court registry in the municipality where the land is, if there is one there. If not, it's filed at a registry in the judicial district. Applications are heard at that registry (Law and Equity Act, s. 21).

Court Services Online is B.C.'s electronic court registry. Anyone can search it. Supreme Court civil files show the file number, registry, party names and the list of filed documents. Foreclosures are their own file class. It's a good way to see where a file is at.

blocks.text: What this means when you're buying

parts.t: With a court ordered sale, the seller is the party with conduct of sale, not someone who has lived in the home. So I always plan for your own inspection and your own checks on title, strata documents and property details before the hearing. Your deposit and financing need to be ready for the court's timing. Is a court ordered sale the same as a foreclosure?
In B.C., they're closely linked. The foreclosure is the court process, and a court ordered sale is how the property usually gets sold during it.
How long is the redemption period?
There isn't a fixed length. The court sets it in each case.
Can I buy before the redemption period ends?
Yes. The party with conduct of sale can ask the court to approve a sale before the redemption period is over.
Can someone else outbid me after my offer is accepted?
Yes. Other buyers can bring sealed bids to the approval hearing, and the judge decides which offer to approve.
Practice Direction 66 says sealed bids must be collected in the courtroom by 9:45 a.m. on the day of the hearing.
The court can set a reserve or minimum price when it gives directions for the sale.
How can I check the court file?
Search the file on Court Services Online, B.C.'s electronic court registry.
